text:
Good evening, Burlington. Sunset is at 4:28, but with the clouds thick overhead there won't be much color to catch. Temperatures are hovering in the low 40s as the light fades, and a few spits of rain are still around.

As it cools tonight, that rain turns to a rain and wet snow mix, mostly between about 7pm and 5am. We're talking under a tenth of an inch, so if anything sticks, it's a coating on grassy spots. Roads and sidewalks should stay just wet. We bottom out near 26 early, then temperatures climb back to around 34 by morning, so there's a chance of a slick spot before the climb.

Tomorrow stays gray, with a leftover flake or two early and a high near 41. Most of the day looks dry, and I'd say it's a good one for errands. Showers could return late Friday night, and the lake might stir up a few around Saturday, though that part is still uncertain. The good news is that drier, milder weather settles in next week, with highs near 50.

AFD DISCUSSION (the forecaster's full reasoning, same regional caveat; their temps are area-wide ranges):
KEY MESSAGE 1: Current radar depicts our parent surface low occluding over western Pennsylvania this afternoon, with RAP surface analysis denoting the secondary coastal low beginning to deepen near the Delaware Bay. This secondary low will become the dominant system tonight into tomorrow with the better forcing and dynamics focused to our south. Models continue to shunt the best moisture profiles to our south where an axis of stronger frontogenesis looks to set up along Long Island to Cape Cod. That said, overrunning precipitation has already overspread much of southern Vermont this afternoon with road cameras showing snow falling across our higher elevations in the southern Greens, mainly above 1500ft. However, below 1500ft, into the area valleys, rain is expected to remain the dominant ptype through much of this event. Drier air along the International Border is helping to stifle much of the northward moisture extent, with precipitation amount trends lowering for areas north of US-2, and have since cut back on PoPs for these areas. Total snow amounts have come down slightly in the mountains with generally 2 to 4 inches, heavily tied to the terrain. A Winter Weather Advisory remains in effect until 10 AM Friday for eastern Addison and Rutland Counties in Vermont, as well as western Essex County in New York. Into tonight, with the combination of dynamical cooling and nighttime cooling, some flakes may be able to mix into the the lower elevations like the Champlain and Connecticut River Valleys. Though surface temperatures in the aforementioned areas will remain at or just above freezing, limiting any accumulations to mainly just grassy surfaces. As the low continues to track east Friday, cyclonic north to northwest flow will develop and keep snow showers in the mountains as upslope snow. KEY MESSAGE 2: North to northwest cyclonic flow will keep moisture wrapping around the coast low late Friday through early Sunday. As boundary layer temperatures cool with cold advection towards late Friday, orographic lift will help sustain snow showers in the upslope favored western facing slopes of the central and northern Greens and Adirondacks. In addition, with lake temperatures becoming 10C warmer than the advective cold air aloft, narrow lake enhanced snow showers may develop downstream of Lake Champlain overnight Friday and during the day Saturday. Areas that may see some additional rain/snow enhancement look to be in the areas along a line from Shelburne to Lincoln. The exact placement and actual development of such a mesoscale lake streamer are still uncertain, but dynamically this synoptic setup is favorable for Lake clouds and subsequent precipitation enhancement. Precipitation totals would be light in the aforementioned areas, with mainly rain northwest of Bristol, and perhaps some locally enhanced snow showers around an inch of snow near Bristol, Lincoln, and the Ripton areas.
